sources.title: Thomas Brady and Colum Watt, Lattices in finite real reflection groups (arXiv:math/0501502, 29-page PDF, author manuscript)
sources.locator: Sections 2-7, printed pp. 2-25, read in the complete extracted text of the 29-page PDF: section 2 (the reflection-length order, moved and fixed spaces, equations (1)-(7)); section 3 (the two commuting classes, the Coxeter element gamma = R1...Rn, the recursion for rho_i, Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3, Notes 3.4-3.5, Theorem 3.7, Corollary 3.8, Lemma 3.9); section 4 (Definition 4.1 and Note 4.2); section 5 (Theorem 5.1, Note 5.2, Definition 5.3, Theorem 5.4, Lemmas 5.5-5.6, Note 5.7); section 6 (Definition 6.1, Proposition 6.2, Corollary 6.3, Note 6.4, Definition 6.5, Propositions 6.6-6.7, Corollary 6.8, Definition 6.9, Lemma 6.10, Proposition 6.11, Corollary 6.12, Examples 6.13-6.14); section 7 (Definition 7.3, Proposition 7.1, Proposition 7.2, Theorem 7.4, Corollary 7.5, Theorem 7.6, Corollary 7.7, Theorem 7.8). Section 8 (generalised associahedra) was read only at the level of its introduction and Definition 8.1.

contents.name: Section 3 setup: the partition of the fundamental reflections into two mutually orthogonal classes and the numbering with Coxeter element gamma = R1...Rn
The explicit formulae for rho_i and the statement that the positive roots are rho_1,...,rho_{nh/2} while the negative roots are rho_{(nh/2)+1},...,rho_{nh} (attributed to Steinberg [13])
Theorem 3.2: gamma*mu_i = mu_i - 2*rho_i for 1 <= i <= nh
Corollary 3.3: (gamma - I)mu_i = -2 rho_i, mu_i . rho_i = 1 and mu_i in F(R(rho_i)gamma)
Note 3.4: mu_i is the unique vector of the one-dimensional space F(R(rho_i)gamma) with mu_i . rho_i = 1
Note 3.5: the mu_i as vertices of a Petrie polygon and the interchange of Petrie vertices with roots under I - gamma
contents.reason: The Petrie-polygon description of the mu_i is a geometric restatement not consumed by any contracted claim of this pair; the pair works with the dual-basis recursion and the Coxeter-plane sector description instead.

contents.name: Theorem 3.7(a)-(d): the antisymmetry mu_i . rho_j = -mu_{j+n} . rho_i, positivity for i <= j, the vanishing mu_{i+t} . rho_i = 0 for 1 <= t <= n-1, and negativity for i < j
Corollary 3.8: an earlier root rho_k is not in the positive cone on earlier positive roots
Lemma 3.9: the factorization criterion l(R(sigma_1)...R(sigma_k)gamma) = n-k iff mu(sigma_i) . sigma_j = 0 for all i > j
Definition 4.1 and Note 4.2: the simplicial complex X(gamma) with vertex set {rho_1,...,rho_nh/2} and the n-k face criterion
Section 5 preamble and Theorem 5.1: P as the positive roots of the reflection group {w : M(w) contained in M(sigma)}, the simple system Delta and the recursive determination of its elements delta_i
Note 5.2: delta_i is the first root in M(R(delta_1)...R(delta_{i-1})sigma), in particular delta_1 = tau_1
Definition 5.3: the fat simplex associated to sigma as the sphere section of the positive cone on the simple system
Theorem 5.4 and Lemma 5.5: the rank-two case l(sigma) = 2 with P = {tau_1,...,tau_t}, the unique two-reflection factorizations of sigma, and the action of R(tau_1) and R(tau_t) on P
Lemma 5.6: for distinct positive roots with R(rho_i)R(rho_j) <= gamma one has rho_i . rho_j <= 0 when i < j and >= 0 when i > j
Note 5.7: the geometric edge criterion (non-obtuse angle plus one ordering of the two reflections preceding gamma)

Definition 6.1, Proposition 6.2 and Corollary 6.3: the roots epsilon_i = R(delta_1)...R(delta_{i-1})delta_i, the factorizations sigma = R(epsilon_k)...R(epsilon_1) and the wall description of the fat simplex by the planes mu(epsilon_i)^perp
Definition 6.5, Propositions 6.6-6.7 and Corollary 6.8: the projected Petrie vertices mu'(tau_i), their duality with the delta_i, and the characterization of the dual basis of the simple system

Definition 6.9, Lemma 6.10, Proposition 6.11 and Corollary 6.12: the reordering theta of the epsilon's, commutativity of the reordered reflections, the factorization sigma = R(theta_k)...R(theta_1) and the lexicographically first top-dimensional simplex of X(sigma)
Examples 6.13 and 6.14: the worked computations of P_sigma, Delta and the epsilon's for the four-dimensional cube group and for A_3
contents.reason: Both worked examples illustrate the general recursion with concrete root data different from this pair's two commissioned computations (I_2(5) and the A_3 model in the page's own bipartite labelling), so neither is needed by a contracted claim.

contents.name: Proposition 7.1: sigma^{-1}(tau_s) lies in -P exactly when tau_s is one of the epsilon_i
Proposition 7.2: the separating-root lemma (two earlier roots of P on the hyperplane mu(tau_a)^perp separated by mu(tau_s)^perp)
Definition 7.3: the halfspaces mu(tau_i)^+, the subcomplex X(sigma,rho), the cones c[X(sigma,rho)] and Y(sigma,rho), and the model cone Z(sigma,tau_i)
Theorem 7.4: X(sigma,tau_i) is a simplicial complex for each i
Corollary 7.5: X(sigma) is a simplicial complex of dimension l(sigma)-1
Theorem 7.6: the identification c[X(sigma,rho)] = Y(sigma,tau_i) = Z(sigma,tau_i) by nested induction on the root index and on l(sigma)
Corollary 7.7: convexity of |X(sigma)| and the two descriptions of |X(sigma)| as a sphere section
Theorem 7.8: the interval [I,gamma] is a lattice in the reflection-length order
contents.reason: The lattice property of the absolute interval is the subject of the later noncrossing-partition page of this run, which consumes the convexity results supplied here; this pair is contracted to supply the ordered root complex and its facet induction, not the lattice theorem itself.

contents.name: Section 8: the embedding of X(gamma) into the larger complex EX(gamma) and the comparison with simplicial generalised associahedra
contents.reason: The associahedron comparison and the spherical-realisation theorem for EX(gamma) belong to the later Cambrian and noncrossing development of the track and are used by no contracted claim of this pair.

sources.title: Robert Steinberg, Finite reflection groups, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 91 (1959) 493-504 (AMS free digital archive PDF)
sources.locator: Sections 2-6, printed pp. 494-501, read in the complete extracted text of the 12-page AMS PDF (article pp. 493-504): Lemmas 2.1-2.3; section 3 (convention 3.1 and Lemmas 3.2-3.6); section 4 (Theorem 4.2, Corollaries 4.3-4.6 and formulas (4.7)-(4.8)); section 5 through Theorem 5.1; and section 6 (Lemma 6.2 and Theorem 6.3 with proof). Sections 7-9 were not read.

contents.name: Lemma 2.2: a graph whose circuits are all even has its nodes in two classes with each link joining distinct classes
Section 3, convention 3.1: the walls W_1,...,W_n of the fundamental simplex ordered so that W_1,...,W_s and W_{s+1},...,W_n are mutually orthogonal
Lemma 3.2 and Lemma 3.6: the extreme-distance description of the product ST as translations along the distinguished lines together with the central inversion
Theorem 4.2: if the product of the reflections in the walls has order h then the number of reflecting hyperplanes is nh/2
Corollary 4.3: the extreme distances are integral multiples of pi/h and exp(2 pi i/h) is a characteristic value
Corollary 4.4: for odd h one has s = n - s, so the two orthogonal classes have equal size
Corollary 4.5: if the central inversion lies in the group then h is even and equals R^{h/2}
Corollary 4.6 with (4.7) and (4.8): the reflecting hyperplanes R_1...R_{k-1}W_k and the reflections R_1...R_k...R_1 for k = 1,...,nh/2
Theorem 5.1: the Petrie polygon vertices B_k = R_1...R_{k-1}e^k are distinct and the nh (n-2)-simplexes lie two in each reflecting hyperplane
Lemma 6.2: a simple reflection negates its fundamental root and permutes the remaining positive roots
Theorem 6.3 with proof: the first nh/2 cyclic prefix roots are positive and the next nh/2 are negative, using the hyperplane ordering of Corollary 4.6 and the reversed ordering for the second half

sources.title: Bill Casselman, Essays on Coxeter groups: Coxeter elements in finite Coxeter groups (author-hosted PDF, 12 pages)
sources.locator: Sections 1 (with Lemmas 1.2-1.4, Theorem 1.5 and Proposition 1.6), 3.1-3.11 and section 4 up to Proposition 4.1, printed pp. 1-3 and 6-10, read in the complete extracted text of the 12-page PDF. The incomplete parts of the essay (its own note that it does not discuss the order formula or polynomial invariants) were not treated as sources.

contents.name: Lemma 1.2: the Coxeter graph of an irreducible finite Coxeter group is a tree
contents.reason: The tree property of the Coxeter graph is consumed here from the in-run diagram page (lem-cg-positive-definite-diagram-exclusions); this alternative proof is not separately needed.

contents.name: Lemma 1.3: the nodes of a finite tree can be numbered so that the first m always span a connected subtree
contents.reason: The pair fixes its root ordering by a bipartition of the tree and needs no compatible node numbering; the lemma's numbering device serves only the survey's own proof of Proposition 1.6.

contents.name: Lemma 1.4: any permutation of a word of distinct generators can be obtained by commuting moves
contents.reason: The well-definedness of the two commuting products a and b follows here directly from B(e_s,e_t) = 0 inside a colour class, so the general commutation move for distinct generators is not consumed.

contents.name: Theorem 1.5 and Proposition 1.6: all Coxeter elements are conjugate and the distinguished element s_1...s_r s_{r+1}...s_n is a product of two involutions
contents.reason: The pair fixes the standard bipartite Coxeter element c = ab and proves directly that the two class products are well defined; conjugacy of arbitrary Coxeter elements is used by no claim of this page.

contents.name: Proposition 3.2: no Coxeter element has eigenvalue 1
contents.reason: Invertibility of c - id is proved here directly from the dual-basis recursion (c - 1)beta_i = -2 rho_i and the triangular independence of rho_1,...,rho_n; the eigenvalue-free restatement is not separately consumed.

contents.name: Lemma 3.3: the matrix identity 2I + gamma + gamma^{-1} = 4(I - A)^2 in simple-root coordinates
contents.reason: The rotation angle of c on the Coxeter plane is identified in this pair by the trace and determinant of c|_P in the basis (u,v) together with the sector count; the survey's matrix identity is an alternative route and is not needed.

contents.name: Proposition 3.7 and Lemma 3.8: the pairing of conjugate eigenvalue pairs of gamma with eigenvalues of A, and the action of the two class involutions on a rotation plane as reflections at angle theta/2
Lemmas 3.9-3.10: one-dimensionality of the critical eigenspace of A by Perron-Frobenius
Theorem 3.11: the Coxeter element acts on the plane spanned by the positive eigenvector as a rotation through 2 pi/h

Section 4 up to Proposition 4.1: the explicit coordinates of the Coxeter plane, the uniqueness of the two reflections, and the identification of the plane sector with the intersection of the plane with the fundamental chamber

sources.title: Sergey Fomin and Nathan Reading, Root systems and generalized associahedra, IAS/Park City Mathematics Series lecture notes (arXiv:math/0505518, 69-page PDF)
sources.locator: Section 2.5 'Coxeter element and Coxeter number', printed pp. 22-24 with Figures 2.5-2.7: the bipartite structure of a finite Coxeter diagram, the well-defined Coxeter element c, Example 2.16 for A_5, the fixed two-dimensional plane L and the Coxeter number h, Examples 2.17 (A_3, h = 4) and 2.18 (B_3). Read in the complete extracted text of the 69-page PDF; the remaining sections were consulted only for orientation.

contents.name: The underlying graph of a finite Coxeter diagram has no cycles, hence is bipartite: I = I+ disjoint-union I- with each part totally disconnected, and the product c = (prod over I+) (prod over I-) is well defined
The Coxeter element fixes a two-dimensional plane L setwise, and its action on L determines its order, the Coxeter number h
Example 2.16: the A_5 Coxeter element c = s_2 s_4 s_1 s_3 s_5 written in the interleaved convention
contents.reason: The A_5 illustration uses the interleaved presentation of a general Coxeter element; the pair's only commissioned computations are the I_2(5) and A_3 models in the page's own bipartite labelling.

contents.name: Examples 2.17 and 2.18: the A_3 and B_3 Coxeter planes and the orders h = 4 and h = 6
contents.reason: The A_3 and B_3 plane pictures illustrate the general plane statement; the pair computes its A_3 instance from the coordinate model of its own example and does not consume the printed figures.
